cells.tense: The understanding here is complete, and your hand is the one on the pen.
cells.act: count it out and read what the numbers show
cells.ask: Total up a goal you're moving toward — what went in, what came back, what's left. Take the figures at face value and make the next move from them.
cells.core:
The goal you're driving at is fully in view. No part of it hidden, nothing left to work out about where it's going. You act on what you understand, and the understanding stays yours. That's why direction holds under resistance without burning you up.
A finished picture has another use in it, and it isn't more looking. Add the goal up: what you've spent, what's returned, what remains. The figures won't match what you assumed they would. Take them at face value, and make the next move from what they say instead of the plan you've been carrying. Running the logic once, on paper, is what full understanding can still do while it's fresh. When it gets used, clarity keeps paying after it's complete.
cells.sheetLine: You understand the whole thing. Now total it up.
cells.verb: seeing something through to its finish
cells.place: in directed momentum toward a goal

cells.tense: You will have finished the thing in your head before it has started.
cells.act: catch the first spark before you point it anywhere
cells.ask: Catch the first flicker of the next thing before it has a name, and carry it a day without aiming it at any goal.
cells.core:
Where you drive now, what you understand has outrun the work itself. You reach the end in your mind before the first step is taken, and the small move today looks pointless next to a finish you already possess. The clarity is genuine — that's what makes it hard. It's covering ground not yet walked, and momentum stalls under a settlement already reached.
A spark is real before it has a shape. Let the next thing stay nameless for a day: no target, no deadline, no long-range plan. Do the small task anyway, keeping the outcome deliberately out of sight. Understanding confirms direction once movement exists; it isn't what starts the engine. Check the aim after the first steps, not before them.
cells.sheetLine: You've finished it in your head before starting it.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door the decision already passed through.
cells.act: define the seed of what will be built, in one line
cells.ask: Put the waiting goal into a single sentence — what it's for — and take the next day's step inside that sentence alone.
cells.core:
Where you push now, the vision has gone tired. The goal is visible through old glass — it stopped being sharp somewhere and you only half remember it — and the momentum runs on habit instead of direction. You still show up. Nothing in you arrives while you do, and what energy is left keeps draining backward into what's already done.
Direction doesn't come back through more force. It comes back by getting small. Put the goal into a single sentence — what this is for, not the whole plan — and treat that sentence as complete. Take the next day's step inside it, without asking the step to feel right. Choosing from something clear is what refreshes the will; the clear thing can be one sentence long. Direction feeds the movement, not the effort.
cells.sheetLine: You keep moving, but toward a picture gone dim.

cells.tense: You have already written this moment and don't count as its author.
cells.act: let this moment be a fresh entry, not a continuation
cells.ask: Start the next step as a first step — not the next in a series, and not evidence for anything you've already done.
cells.core:
Where you push now, what you understand works so smoothly that you've stopped claiming it. You read the goal exactly, act on it exactly, and call the result inevitable, or the plan's, or simply what someone like you does. The driving is happening — your hands are on it — and none of it feels authored.
Each push enters from where you're standing, not from the ledger of the ones before. Take the next step as a first one: not proof of a history, not another unit in a long sequence. The goal out there stays the goal, and the move toward it is written new the moment you make it. That isn't a compliment you owe yourself. It's what was going on the entire time, before you filed it under something else.
cells.sheetLine: The push is yours, and you've been calling it the plan's.

attempts.check: The statuses of this signature are the derivations of its parent's, so the reading of the card in the Drive seat is the same as the reading of the parent's in that seat; this is a reading of the signature's own status face. The reader could reasonably say the Too Much and Too Little cells describe the pausing of the drive rather than a distortion of it, and the Too Little cell's 'placing yourself where the only choice is the one already made' could read as pushing effort into the empty seat; it is not — it is a resource given back to the drive's own action, not a demand for effort or feeling. The asks survive being wrong: each is the filling of a drive with a resource the medicine gives, and none is conditional on the read. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person: 'the person needs to be more decisive.' It has been cut. The asks are the partners' own acts, done small, in the Drive seat — no other person is needed or required in any of them.
